285→
   286→The API runs in the same process as the protocol processor and **calls the Vertex AI endpoint** for MedGemma. It needs: database (Cloud SQL), secrets (Session/JWT), and IAM to use Vertex AI and Secret Manager.
   287→
   288→### 4.1 Create API secrets (Session, JWT)
   289→
   290→```bash
   291→# Generate and store session secret
   292→openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' | gcloud secrets create api-session-secret --data-file=-
   293→
   294→# Generate and store JWT secret
   295→openssl rand -base64 32 | tr -d '\n' | gcloud secrets create api-jwt-secret --data-file=-
   296→```
   297→
   298→### 4.2 Build and push the API image
   299→
   300→From the **repository root**. Use the Cloud Build config (it specifies the Dockerfile path; `gcloud builds submit` does not accept `-f` directly):
   301→
   302→```bash
   303→cd /path/to/medgemma-hackathon-main
   304→
   305→gcloud builds submit --config=cloudbuild-api.yaml --substitutions=_REGION=${REGION} .
   306→```
   307→
   308→### 4.3 Build DATABASE_URL for Cloud SQL
   309→
   310→For Cloud Run + Cloud SQL Unix socket, the URL format is:
   311→
   312→```text
   313→postgresql://USER:PASSWORD@/DATABASE?host=/cloudsql/CONNECTION_NAME
   314→```
   315→
   316→If you use Secret Manager only for the password, you can either:
   317→
   318→- Store the **full** `DATABASE_URL` in a secret (e.g. `db-url`), or  
   319→- Pass non-secret parts as env vars and the password as a secret (e.g. `DB_PASSWORD`), and build the URL in the app if you add support for that.
   320→
   321→Simplest for this guide: create a secret that holds the full URL:
   322→
   323→```bash
   324→# Replace USER, PASSWORD, DATABASE, CONNECTION_NAME
   325→export DATABASE_URL="postgresql://${DB_USER}:${DB_PASSWORD}@/${DB_NAME}?host=/cloudsql/${CONNECTION_NAME}"
   326→echo -n "$DATABASE_URL" | gcloud secrets create db-url --data-file=-
   327→# If secret already exists, add a new version:
   328→# echo -n "$DATABASE_URL" | gcloud secrets versions add db-url --data-file=-
   329→```
   330→
   331→### 4.3a Create GCS bucket (before API deploy)
   332→
   333→Create the bucket for protocol PDFs and grant the Cloud Run API service account access **before** deploying the API so the first revision already has a working GCS backend.
   334→
   335→```bash
   336→# Cloud Run will use the default compute service account (same as in 4.5)
   337→export PROJECT_NUMBER=$(gcloud projects describe $PROJECT_ID --format='value(projectNumber)')
   338→export API_SA="${PROJECT_NUMBER}-compute@developer.gserviceaccount.com"
   339→
   340→# Bucket name used in the deploy command (4.4)
   341→export GCS_BUCKET_NAME="${GCS_BUCKET_NAME:-${PROJECT_ID}-api-protocols}"
   342→
   343→# Create bucket (same region as Cloud Run)
   344→gsutil mb -l $REGION gs://${GCS_BUCKET_NAME}
   345→
   346→# Grant the API service account read/write on the bucket
   347→gsutil iam ch serviceAccount:${API_SA}:objectAdmin gs://${GCS_BUCKET_NAME}
   348→```
   349→
   350→Keep `GCS_BUCKET_NAME` and `API_SA` set for the next steps (4.4 and 4.5).
   351→
   352→### 4.4 Deploy the API service
   353→
   354→Replace placeholders with your values. The API will use the **default Cloud Run service account**; we will grant it roles in the next section. On first deploy you can omit `CORS_ORIGINS` (or set it to a placeholder); set it to your **frontend** URL after deploying the frontend (step 4.6).
   355→
   356→**For one command that regroups all secrets and env vars**, see **section 4.4b**.
   357→
   358→**Migrations:** The container startup runs `alembic upgrade head` before starting the API (in the Dockerfile CMD). It uses `DATABASE_URL` from the environment (injected from the `db-url` secret). Migrations run automatically on every deploy; you do not need to run them manually on the Cloud SQL instance.
   359→
   360→**Port:** The container listens on the `PORT` environment variable (Cloud Run sets `PORT=8080`). The Dockerfile uses `--port ${PORT:-8000}` so it works on Cloud Run and locally.
   361→
   362→```bash
   363→# GCS_BUCKET_NAME from 4.3a (bucket already created and IAM granted)
   364→gcloud run deploy api \
   365→  --image ${REGION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT_ID}/app-images/api:latest \
   366→  --region $REGION \
   367→  --platform managed \
   368→  --allow-unauthenticated \
   369→  --add-cloudsql-instances $CONNECTION_NAME \
   370→  --set-env-vars "ENVIRONMENT=production" \
   371→  --set-env-vars "GCP_PROJECT_ID=${PROJECT_ID}" \
   372→  --set-env-vars "GCP_REGION=${REGION}" \
   373→  --set-env-vars "MODEL_BACKEND=vertex" \
   374→  --set-env-vars "REDACTED" \
   375→  --set-env-vars "GCS_BUCKET_NAME=${GCS_BUCKET_NAME}" \
   376→  --set-env-vars "USE_LOCAL_STORAGE=0" \
   377→  --set-secrets "DATABASE_URL=db-url:latest" \
   378→  --set-secrets "SESSION_SECRET=api-session-secret:latest" \
   379→  --set-secrets "JWT_SECRET_KEY=api-jwt-secret:latest"
   380→```
   381→
   382→- **Vertex**: Set `VERTEX_ENDPOINT_ID` (and optionally `VERTEX_MODEL_NAME`) to your deployed MedGemma endpoint. The API calls Vertex via the default credential chain (Cloud Run service account).
   383→- **CORS**: Set `CORS_ORIGINS` to your frontend URL(s). After you deploy the frontend, update the API revision with the real frontend URL (see below).
   384→- **Optional env vars**: `GEMINI_MODEL_NAME` (e.g. `gemini-2.5-flash`), `UMLS_API_KEY`, `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` as needed. For **Gemini** (extraction + structuring), set `GOOGLE_API_KEY` via Secret Manager — see section **4.4a**. For health to report **gcs** and **omop_vocab** as available, set `GCS_BUCKET_NAME` and `OMOP_VOCAB_URL`; see section 4.6.
   385→
   386→After deploy, note the service URL:
   387→
   388→```bash
   389→gcloud run services describe api --region $REGION --format='value(status.url)'
   390→export API_SERVICE_URL=$(gcloud run services describe api --region $REGION --format='value(status.url)')
   391→```
   392→
   393→**If deploy fails with "Permission denied on secret" for db-url, api-session-secret, or api-jwt-secret:** the Cloud Run revision service account (default compute SA) needs **Secret Manager Secret Accessor**. Run the IAM step below (4.5), then redeploy.
   394→
   395→**Vertex AI (MedGemma) — understanding `/health` and troubleshooting**
   396→
   397→In `/health`, **`breakers.vertex_ai`** is the circuit breaker state for Vertex AI (MedGemma). **`"closed"` is the normal, healthy state** (requests are allowed). **`"open"`** means the breaker tripped after repeated failures. So **`"vertex_ai": "closed"` means OK**, not a problem.
   398→
   399→If **Vertex calls fail at runtime** (e.g. 403, "endpoint not found" when running a protocol):
   400→
   401→1. **Env vars** — Use `VERTEX_ENDPOINT_ID` = **endpoint ID only** (e.g. the numeric ID from the Vertex AI console), not the full resource name. The code builds `projects/{project}/locations/{region}/endpoints/{VERTEX_ENDPOINT_ID}`. Set `GCP_PROJECT_ID` and `GCP_REGION` to match the endpoint’s project and region (e.g. `europe-west4`).
   402→2. **IAM** — The Cloud Run service account needs **Vertex AI User** (`roles/aiplatform.user`); see 4.5.
   403→3. **Endpoint** — In Cloud Console: Vertex AI → Endpoints; confirm the endpoint is deployed and copy its ID.
   404→4. **Logs** — In Cloud Run logs, when a request triggers MedGemma, look for `PermissionDenied`, `NotFound`, or `InvalidArgument` from the Vertex client.
   405→
   406→**If the API crashes at startup with "DATABASE_URL environment variable is required but not set"**
   407→
   408→You likely ran `gcloud run services update api ... --set-secrets "GOOGLE_API_KEY=..."`. The flag **`--set-secrets`** replaces *all* secrets with only the ones you list, so DATABASE_URL (and SESSION_SECRET, JWT_SECRET_KEY) were removed. Restore all required secrets in one go:
   409→
   410→```bash
   411→gcloud run services update api --region $REGION \
   412→  --set-secrets "DATABASE_URL=db-url:latest,SESSION_SECRET=api-session-secret:latest,JWT_SECRET_KEY=api-jwt-secret:latest,GOOGLE_API_KEY=google-api-key:latest"
   413→```
   414→
   415→To only *add* Gemini without touching existing secrets, use **`--update-secrets`** (see 4.4a).
   416→
   417→**If the API revision fails with "container failed to start and listen on the port defined by PORT=8080"**
   418→
   419→Cloud Run reports this when the container never binds to `PORT=8080` within its startup window (or crashes before doing so). Common causes:
   420→
   421→1. **Startup crash** — The container runs `alembic upgrade head` then `uvicorn ... --port ${PORT:-8000}`. If Alembic fails (e.g. `DATABASE_URL` missing or unreachable, migration error) or the app crashes on import (e.g. missing/forbidden secret), the process exits before listening.
   422→2. **Slow startup** — DB in another region, many migrations, or heavy imports can exceed Cloud Run’s startup timeout (~240s); the platform then assumes the container failed to start.
   423→
   424→**What to do:**
   425→
   426→- **Check logs** for the failing revision:  
   427→  **Cloud Run → api → Logs**, or:  
   428→  `gcloud run services logs read api --region $REGION --limit 200`  
   429→  Look for Python tracebacks, `OperationalError`/connection errors (Alembic/DB), or Secret Manager permission errors. If you just added `GOOGLE_API_KEY`, ensure the API service account has **Secret Manager Secret Accessor** and that the secret name is `google-api-key` (see 4.5 and 4.4a).
   430→- **Confirm PORT** — The Dockerfile uses `--port ${PORT:-8000}` and `--host 0.0.0.0`; no change needed for Cloud Run’s `PORT=8080`.
   431→- **Roll back** — If the failure started after an `update` (e.g. adding a secret), route traffic back to the last working revision:  
   432→  `gcloud run revisions list --service api --region $REGION` to get the revision name, then  
   433→  `gcloud run services update-traffic api --region $REGION --to-revisions REVISION_NAME=100`.  
   434→  Then fix the new revision (secrets, IAM, or DB) and redeploy.
   435→- **Slow startup** — Reduce work before listen: run migrations in a one-off job or at build time; keep DB in the same region as Cloud Run; avoid heavy import-time work. Cloud Run’s startup timeout is not configurable (~240s).
   436→
   437→**How to debug when the container fails to start (and logs are empty or hard to find)**
   438→
   439→1. **Logs for the failing revision**  
   440→   Use the revision name from the error (e.g. `api-00009-sx8`):
   441→
   442→   ```bash
   443→   gcloud run services logs read api --region $REGION --limit 300
   444→   ```
   445→
   446→   To filter by revision:
   447→
   448→   ```bash
   449→   gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" resource.labels.service_name="api" resource.labels.revision_name="api-00009-sx8"' --limit 100 --format="table(timestamp,textPayload)" --project $PROJECT_ID
   450→   ```
   451→
   452→   In **Cloud Console**: **Logging → Logs Explorer**. Use query:
   453→
   454→   ```
   455→   resource.type="cloud_run_revision"
   456→   resource.labels.service_name="api"
   457→   resource.labels.revision_name="api-00009-sx8"
   458→   ```
   459→
   460→   Replace `api-00009-sx8` with your failing revision. If no entries appear, try without `revision_name` and look at the latest timestamps; logs can be delayed a few minutes.
   461→
   462→2. **Run the same image locally**  
   463→   This reproduces the crash on your machine so you see the traceback in the terminal:
   464→
   465→   ```bash
   466→   export REGION=europe-west4
   467→   export PROJECT_ID=your-project-id
   468→   docker pull ${REGION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT_ID}/app-images/api:latest
   469→   # Get secrets (you need access to the project)
   470→   export DATABASE_URL=$(gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=db-url)
   471→   export SESSION_SECRET=$(gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=api-session-secret)
   472→   export JWT_SECRET_KEY=$(gcloud secrets versions access latest --secret=api-jwt-secret)
   473→   # Optional: GOOGLE_API_KEY, OMOP_VOCAB_URL
   474→   docker run --rm -e PORT=8080 -e ENVIRONMENT=production -e GCP_PROJECT_ID=$PROJECT_ID -e GCP_REGION=$REGION \
   475→     -e MODEL_BACKEND=vertex -e VERTEX_ENDPOINT_ID=your-endpoint -e GCS_BUCKET_NAME=your-bucket -e USE_LOCAL_STORAGE=0 \
   476→     -e DATABASE_URL -e SESSION_SECRET -e JWT_SECRET_KEY -p 8080:8080 \
   477→     ${REGION}-docker.pkg.dev/${PROJECT_ID}/app-images/api:latest
   478→   ```
   479→
   480→   If the app needs Cloud SQL, run **Cloud SQL Proxy** in another terminal and use `DATABASE_URL` with `localhost` (and the proxy port) instead of the Cloud SQL socket. The container will crash with the same error as on Cloud Run (e.g. `ValueError: DATABASE_URL ... not set` or a DB connection error), and you’ll see it in the terminal.
   481→
   482→3. **Run the API without Docker (from repo)**

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Cloud Run cold starts, scaling to zero, and related issues:

## Cold Starts and Scale to Zero

When Cloud Run scales to zero (no active instances), the first request triggers a cold start, which means Google Cloud must start a new container, load the model, and initialize the runtime. Cold starts are what make scale to zero possible, ensuring you pay nothing when the service is idle.

## Connection Issues and Service Unavailability

Logs show error messages about connection problems, such as failures, timeouts, or refused connections, and these logs often reveal if the connection issue is with your application or the network.

## Mitigating Cold Starts

Several strategies can help address cold start issues:

1. **Minimum Instances**: Configure minimum instances to reduce the amount of cold starts with a higher billing implication.

2. **Scheduled Requests**: You can work around "cold starts" by periodically making requests to your Cloud Run service which can help prevent the container instances from scaling to zero, using Google Cloud Scheduler to make requests every few minutes.

3. **Code Optimization**: Cold starts include image boot, dependency load, and application initialization, and apps with large dependency trees, database connections, or cold SDK clients during boot increase startup duration.

4. **Container Design**: Use minimal base images (e.g., Alpine, Distroless), remove unnecessary files, and reduce dependency weight to accelerate boot time.

The search results don't contain specific information about MLflow connection refused errors during cold starts, but the general connection troubleshooting and cold start mitigation strategies above would apply to that scenario as well.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Tenacity, retry logic in Python, asyncio, and FastAPI:

## Tenacity Library Overview

Tenacity is an Apache 2.0 licensed general-purpose retrying library, written in Python, to simplify the task of adding retry behavior to just about anything. The latest version 9.1.4 was released on Feb 7, 2026, with version 9.1.2 released on April 2, 2025.

## Asyncio Support

Tenacity's retry works on asyncio coroutines with asynchronous sleeps. With async code you can use AsyncRetrying. Here's an example:

With async code you can use AsyncRetrying, which allows you to configure retry policies for async functions that raise exceptions.

## FastAPI Integration

If the API or resource you are making a query to is flaky, using a retry library such as Tenacity is a good idea. HTTPX is the preferred request library for FastAPI and is installed when FastAPI is installed. You can combine HTTPX with Tenacity for async requests in FastAPI applications.

## Key Features

Tenacity requires Python >=3.10 and supports Python 3.10 through 3.14. The library offers extensive customization options including stop conditions (like `stop_after_attempt`), wait strategies (like `wait_exponential`), and retry conditions based on exceptions or return values.

## Overview

mlflow-skinny is a lightweight MLflow package without SQL storage, server, UI, or data science dependencies. Additional dependencies can be installed to leverage the full feature set of MLflow.

## Supported Features

MLflow Skinny supports tracking operations (logging/loading/searching params, metrics, tags + logging/loading artifacts), model registration, search, artifact loading, and deployment, as well as execution of GitHub projects within notebook & against a remote target.

## Key Benefits

- **Lightweight Installation**: MLflow Skinny minimizes the number of third-party dependencies, making it easier to install and manage.
- **Reduced Resource Usage**: It requires less storage and compute power, ideal for scenarios with limited resources.
- **Compatibility**: MLflow Skinny is compatible with the main MLflow package, ensuring that users can switch between the two versions as needed.

## Recommended Use Cases

mlflow-skinny is recommended for users who primarily need the MLflow tracking and logging capabilities but not the full suite of features, including deployments.

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about the comma delimiter pitfall with `gcloud run deploy --set-env-vars`. Here's what I found:

## The Comma Delimiter Pitfall

The comma character (,) is used to split environment variables, and if your environment variable contains comma characters as values, you need to escape those delimiters by specifying a different delimiter character.

### The Problem

If you pass a comma to gcloud, it will treat the comma (,) character as another environment variable declaration and will try to split the value into multiple environment variables.

### The Solution

You can specify a different delimiter character, for example, @: --set-env-vars "^@^KEY1=value1,value2,value3@KEY2=..."

This is particularly important for CORS URL configurations, which often contain commas in their values (for multiple origin URLs).

### Common Examples

When trying to use commas in --set-env-vars values without escaping them with a custom delimiter, it causes parsing errors. For instance, if your values contain commas, you can use ^##^ syntax to specify a custom delimiter to avoid parsing issues: --set-env-vars ^##^API_KEY=abc,123^##^DATABASE_URL=postgres://db

### Best Practices

To avoid issues, you should not cram all environment variables into a single option, prevent your shell from interpreting arguments as much as you can, and if things are getting out of control, switch to a declarative resource model with YAML.

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about Cloud Run YAML service manifests and declarative deployment with `gcloud run services replace`:

## Cloud Run YAML Service Manifest Structure

The YAML representation describes the Cloud Run service and job objects, which maps directly to the Cloud Run Admin API V1.

A basic Cloud Run service YAML follows the Knative API format:

A Knative Service manifest includes apiVersion: serving.knative.dev/v1, kind: Service, metadata with name and annotations, and a spec section with container configuration, resources, and environment variables.

## Declarative Deployment with `gcloud run services replace`

The `gcloud run services replace` command is used to deploy the service, which applies the YAML manifest to create a new service or revision. Both `gcloud run services replace` and the deploy-cloudrun action use declarative knative API that makes sure that all the parameters of the service (including the image name) are as described in the YAML file.

You can leverage the `gcloud run services replace` command to update the running Cloud Run service, and the command syntax is: `gcloud run services replace service.yaml --region REGION`.

## Key Advantages

You can deploy your entire Cloud Run service from a manifest file written in YAML because Cloud Run services are actually Knative API objects, which is done with the `gcloud run services replace` command.

This declarative approach provides infrastructure-as-code capabilities for reproducible, version-controlled Cloud Run deployments.

Based on the search results, I've found comprehensive information about the Cloud Run min-instances vs scale-to-zero cost tradeoff. While the results don't contain specific information about MLflow tracking servers, the general principles apply to any stateful or latency-sensitive services. Here's what the research shows:

## The Cost Tradeoff

Instances kept running using the minimum instances feature do incur billing costs. For request-based billing, you are billed at a lower rate when instances are idle and waiting to process requests. If min instances is set to 0, you are not billed when instances are idle.

## When to Use Min-Instances

If you need more control over your service's autoscaling behavior, you can set a minimum number of instances to avoid slow container start times and reduce service latency. You can change the default behavior by specifying a minimum number of container instances to be kept warm and ready to serve requests.

If your service is using CPU even when it's not processing requests, you should set minimum instances equal to 1. This would apply to services like MLflow tracking servers that may need background processing.

## Latency vs Cost Balance

Cloud Run min instances can enable more off-the-shelf applications to run under the serverless model and be more cost efficient—and give you more control over the trade-offs inherent in serverless compute. Instead of allowing the system to enable scale-to-zero automatically, you can set a predetermined minimum instance amount. This approach allows you to guarantee low latency when configuring critical services.

## Cold Start Costs

Scaling from zero can only be triggered by a request, so a service that is not processing requests cannot scale from zero. For these workloads, you can either set minimum instances > 0, or include a "wake-up request" in your design to restart processing after scaling to zero.

For an MLflow tracking server specifically, min-instances would likely be worthwhile since tracking servers typically need to be responsive and available for experiments to log metrics without incurring startup delays.

I've completed the web search for your query about Cloud Run environment-aware configuration with Secret Manager best practices. Here are the key findings:

## Key Best Practices

**Environment Segmentation:**
Segment applications and environments (staging or production) into separate projects to help isolate environments with project level IAM binding and ensure that quotas are enforced independently.

**Secret Version Handling:**
Environment variables are resolved at instance startup time, so Google recommends that you pin the secret to a particular version instead of using latest as the version. For production, it's safer to pin to a specific version (e.g., POSTGRES_PASSWORD:1).

**Secret Access Control:**
Choose a curated-role with the minimal necessary permissions, or create a custom role if necessary. When secrets for many services are in a single project, use secret level IAM bindings, or IAM Conditions to limit access to the necessary subset of secrets.

**Security Considerations:**
When a secret is consumed through environment variables, misconfigurations such as enabling debug endpoints or including dependencies that log process environment details may leak secrets. Secret Manager stores secrets in an encrypted format and provides access through tightly controlled IAM permissions, which is much more secure than plain text environment variables.

**Secret Rotation:**
Periodically rotate your secrets to limit the impact in the case of a leaked secret, ensure that individuals who no longer require access to a secret can't continue to use a previously accessed secret, and reduce the likelihood of an outage.

The search results provide comprehensive documentation from Google Cloud on configuring Cloud Run services with Secret Manager for secure production and staging environments.

# MLflow Production Tracing SDK

## What It Is

The Production Tracing SDK, called `mlflow-tracing`, is a lightweight package designed for production environments. According to the documentation, it "includes only the essential functionality for tracing and monitoring of your GenAI applications."

## Key Differences from Full MLflow

The lightweight version is dramatically smaller and more focused:

- **Size**: "95% smaller" than full MLflow (~5MB vs ~1000MB)
- **Dependencies**: Includes only 5-8 packages versus 20+ in the full version
- **Scope**: Provides tracing and observability features exclusively

Full MLflow capabilities NOT included in the SDK:
- Run management APIs (`mlflow.start_run()`, `mlflow.log_metric()`)
- Model logging and evaluation
- Model Registry
- MLflow Projects and Recipes
- Tracking Server UI

## Installation

Install via pip:

```bash
pip install mlflow-tracing
```

**Important warning**: "Do not install the full `mlflow` package together with the `mlflow-tracing` package, as this may cause version conflicts and namespace resolution issues."

The documentation doesn't specify a particular version number—it appears to use the standard pip installation without version constraints mentioned.

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about the `MLFLOW_ENABLE_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING` environment variable:

## Overview

The `MLFLOW_ENABLE_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING` environment variable specifies whether to enable async trace logging to Databricks Tracing Server.

## Purpose and Benefits

By default, MLflow Traces are logged synchronously, which may introduce a performance overhead when logging Traces, especially when your MLflow Tracking Server is running on a remote server. You can enable asynchronous logging for tracing in MLflow 2.16.0 and later, which will make the trace logging operation non-blocking and reduce the performance overhead.

## Production Configuration

For production environments, it's recommended to configure async logging along with related settings like `MLFLOW_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING_MAX_WORKERS=10` and `MLFLOW_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING_MAX_QUEUE_SIZE=1000`.

## Default Value

The default value is True.

## Related Configuration Options

When using async trace logging, you can also configure:
- Maximum number of spans to export in a single batch with `MLFLOW_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING_MAX_SPAN_BATCH_SIZE`, which will export spans in batches when set to larger than 1.
- Maximum number of worker threads with `MLFLOW_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING_MAX_WORKERS` (default: 10) and timeout seconds for retrying trace logging with `MLFLOW_ASYNC_TRACE_LOGGING_RETRY_TIMEOUT` (default: 500).

Based on the search results, here's comprehensive information about Cloud Run's CPU allocation options for background processing:

## CPU Allocation Modes

Cloud Run offers two billing and CPU allocation models:

**Request-Based Billing (Default):**
With request-based billing, CPU is only allocated during request processing. Request-based billing only charges your Cloud Run instances during request processing, container startup, and container shutdown.

**Instance-Based Billing (Always Allocated):**
With instance-based billing, CPU is allocated for the entire container instance lifecycle. Instance-based billing charges your Cloud Run instances for the entire lifecycle of instances, even when there are no incoming requests.

## Background Processing with Outbox Pattern

Selecting instance-based billing allocates CPU even outside of request processing, letting you execute short-lived background tasks and other asynchronous processing work after returning responses. Combining instance-based billing with a number of minimum instances results in a number of instances up and running with full access to CPU resources, enabling background processing use cases. When using this pattern, Cloud Run applies instance autoscaling even if a service is using CPU outside of any requests.

## Use Case Recommendations

Request-based billing is recommended when incoming traffic is sporadic, bursty or spiky. Instance-based billing is recommended when incoming traffic is steady, slowly varying. With "CPU always allocated," your container can use CPU even between requests, which helps with connection pooling, background tasks, and warming caches.

## Pricing Considerations

CPU is priced 25% lower and memory 20% lower with always-allocated mode compared to on-demand pricing. However, using 'Always allocated' means you pay for CPU even when the container is idle, which significantly increases costs for services with sporadic traffic.

I found several highly relevant resources about httpx async Python timeout and retry best practices for 2025. Here's what the search results reveal:

## Key Best Practices

**Connection Management:**
Recreating clients per request kills connection reuse and TLS handshakes. Use one long-lived AsyncClient and share it.

**Timeout Configuration:**
HTTPX is careful to enforce timeouts everywhere by default. The default behavior is to raise a TimeoutException after 5 seconds of network inactivity. You can set specific hard limits with individual connect, read, write, and pool timeout values (e.g., connect=3.0, read=5.0, write=5.0, pool=3.0).

**Retry Strategies:**
Requests will be retried the given number of times in case an httpx.ConnectError or an httpx.ConnectTimeout occurs, allowing smoother operation under flaky networks. However, if you need other forms of retry behaviors, such as handling read/write errors or reacting to 503 Service Unavailable, consider general-purpose tools such as tenacity.

**Exponential Backoff with Jitter:**
One of the best practices is to use a backoff strategy, where the delay increases with each consecutive retry, reducing the risk of overwhelming the server and increasing the chances of successful execution. Combined with jitter (randomness), this prevents thundering herd problems where all clients retry simultaneously.

**Rate Limiting & Retry-After Headers:**
HTTP 429 Too Many Requests should retry after rate limit cooldown (respect Retry-After header when available), as should 500, 502, and 504 errors for service-to-service communication.

The search results include recent 2025 resources on production-ready patterns using httpx with asyncio for building resilient service-to-service communication.

content.content:
# Status of Refreshable MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN Feature

## Current Status
The feature request has been **closed as completed**. A pull request (#8879) was merged to address this issue.

## Key Finding
Interestingly, the MLflow team discovered that **the feature already works without explicit implementation**. As one team member demonstrated, simply updating the environment variable refreshes the token:

> "tokens are read on-the-fly from configs, including environmental variables. Furthermore, these configs can also be changed on the fly"

## Practical Workaround
Users can refresh tokens by directly modifying the environment variable during execution:

```python
os.environ['MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN'] = new_token
```

This approach automatically picks up the new token on subsequent MLflow API calls since the library reads authentication credentials dynamically rather than caching them at initialization.

## Implications
This design eliminates the need for an explicit `mlflow.refresh_token()` API method. Users experiencing token expiration during long-running jobs can simply update the environment variable, and MLflow will use the refreshed credentials for the next operation.

## request_auth_provider Plugin for Custom Authentication

MLflow provides a `RequestAuthProvider` class that can be used to create custom authentication providers. The plugin implements a `get_name()` method to return the provider name and a `get_auth()` method that returns an authentication object for HTTP requests (accepting anything that `requests.auth` accepts).

## Example Implementation

A custom authentication class can add authentication headers to requests, such as Bearer tokens, by implementing a `__call__` method that modifies the request headers and includes token retrieval logic.

## Cloud Run ID Token Usage

While the search results mention that Google Cloud Run has direct support for JWT and automatically passes the user's identity in the email field of specific headers when authentication is enabled, the specific integration of Cloud Run ID tokens with the `request_auth_provider` plugin is not explicitly documented in the search results.

For a production implementation using Cloud Run ID tokens, you would need to fetch the ID token from the Cloud Run metadata service and include it in the Bearer token within your custom provider's authentication logic.

I've performed a web search on Cloud Run health check configuration for startup and liveness probes. Here are the key findings:

## Overview of Startup and Liveness Probes

Cloud Run provides two types of custom health checks, startup and liveness checks.

### Startup Probes
Users can configure startup probes to define when a container has started and is ready to start serving requests. When you configure a startup probe, liveness and readiness checks are disabled until the startup probe determines that the container is started, to prevent interference with the service startup. Startup probes are especially useful if you use liveness checks on slow starting containers, because startup probes prevents the containers from being shut down prematurely before the containers are up and running.

### Liveness Probes
Liveness probes determine whether to restart a container. They should be used primarily for unrecoverable instance failures, such as catching a deadlock where a service is running, but is unable to make progress.

## Supported Probe Types

Cloud Run now supports HTTP, TCP and gRPC probes for startup checks and HTTP and gRPC probes for liveness checks.

## Configuration Details

Add an HTTP/1 endpoint (the Cloud Run default, not HTTP/2) in your service code to respond to the probe. The endpoint name (for example, /startup, /health or /are_you_ready) must match the path in the probe configuration.

## Implementation Example

For an HTTP probe, Cloud Run sends an HTTP GET request to the specified path to perform the check. Probes can be configured with parameters including `initialDelaySeconds`, `failureThreshold`, `timeoutSeconds`, and `periodSeconds`.

1→# MedGemma Deployment Fix
     2→
     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→A clinical trial criteria extraction platform (MedGemma) that currently works locally via Docker Compose but has multiple unresolved issues preventing reliable GCP Cloud Run deployment. The goal is to get the API and frontend deployed and fully operational on Cloud Run without breaking the existing local development workflow.
     6→
     7→## Core Value
     8→
     9→The deployed Cloud Run services must handle the full protocol upload → extraction → review → export pipeline end-to-end, exactly as it works locally.
    10→
    11→## Requirements
    12→
    13→### Validated
    14→
    15→- ✓ Protocol PDF upload via signed GCS URLs — existing
    16→- ✓ 7-node LangGraph extraction pipeline — existing
    17→- ✓ MedGemma + Gemini multi-model grounding — existing
    18→- ✓ Human-in-the-loop review UI — existing
    19→- ✓ CIRCE/FHIR/SQL export — existing
    20→- ✓ Popup OAuth login flow — existing (merge resolved)
    21→- ✓ ProxyHeadersMiddleware for HTTPS behind Cloud Run LB — existing
    22→- ✓ GCS signed URL generation via metadata server — existing
    23→- ✓ CORS with ^||^ delimiter and dual frontend URLs — existing
    24→- ✓ GCS bucket CORS configuration — existing
    25→- ✓ Correct GCS bucket name via GCS_BUCKET_NAME_PROD — existing
    26→
    27→### Active
    28→
    29→- [ ] MLflow service-to-service auth on Cloud Run (403/503 errors)
    30→- [ ] API stability — container becomes unresponsive after deployment
    31→- [ ] Protocol processing completes without dead-lettering (MLflow preflight blocks processing)
    32→- [ ] Deploy script is robust and idempotent
    33→- [ ] Local dev workflow remains unaffected by Cloud Run changes
    34→
    35→### Out of Scope
    36→
    37→- New features beyond deployment — not building new extraction capabilities
    38→- Infrastructure migration — staying on GCP Cloud Run
    39→- MedGemma model retraining — model is already deployed on Vertex AI
    40→- Frontend feature work — UI is complete, just needs to be reachable
    41→
    42→## Context
    43→
    44→The deployment from `feat/revised-prompts` branch encountered 10 issues (documented in `instructions/DEPLOYMENT_ISSUES_REPORT.md`). Issues 1-8 are resolved. The remaining blockers are:
    45→
    46→1. **MLflow Cloud Run service returns 403/503** — The MLflow service deployed on Cloud Run rejects authenticated requests. The API's `_cloud_run_auth.py` fetches ID tokens from the metadata server, but MLflow may not accept Cloud Run ID tokens as Bearer tokens. The MLflow service itself may be unhealthy.
    47→
    48→2. **API becomes unresponsive** — After initial deployment success, the API times out on `/health`. Likely caused by MLflow trace export attempts returning 503 on every request, consuming connections/threads. The deferred MLflow init thread may also hold resources.
    49→
    50→3. **Protocol processing dead-letters** — The `_preflight_check()` in `trigger.py` requires MLflow to be reachable. When MLflow is down, all protocols immediately fail.
    51→
    52→**Key insight:** All three remaining issues stem from MLflow dependency. Making MLflow optional/graceful would likely resolve all of them.
    53→
    54→**Architecture:** FastAPI API + React frontend + PostgreSQL + GCS + LangGraph pipeline + MLflow (optional tracing). Services deploy to Cloud Run in `europe-west4`. Local dev uses Docker Compose.
    55→

    57→- `scripts/deploy_api.sh` — API Cloud Run deploy with env vars
    58→- `scripts/deploy_frontend.sh` — Frontend Cloud Run deploy
    59→

    62→- **Tech stack**: Must stay on GCP Cloud Run, PostgreSQL, GCS — infrastructure already provisioned
    63→- **Compatibility**: All Cloud Run changes must be backward-compatible with Docker Compose local dev
    64→- **Existing code**: Files already modified for deployment (listed in deployment report) — build on those, don't rewrite
    65→- **MLflow**: Cannot guarantee MLflow Cloud Run service is healthy — must degrade gracefully
    66→- **Memory**: Cloud Run API container needs ≥1Gi memory
    67→
    68→## Key Decisions

    71→|----------|-----------|---------|
    72→| Make MLflow optional for protocol processing | MLflow is observability, not core functionality — blocking pipeline on it is wrong | — Pending |
    73→| Disable MLflow autolog trace export if unreachable | Per-request 503s degrade API performance | — Pending |
    74→| Keep deploy scripts as shell scripts | Already exist and work for resolved issues | — Pending |

content.content:
# Custom Authentication for MLflow

Based on the provided documentation, there is **no RequestAuthProvider interface** mentioned. Instead, MLflow offers two approaches:

## Plugin-Based Custom Auth

Create a Python package with an app factory function. The documentation shows this structure:

```python
from flask import Flask, Response, request
from werkzeug.datastructures import Authorization
from mlflow.server import app
from mlflow.server.handlers import catch_mlflow_exception

def authenticate_request_custom() -> Authorization | Response:
    """Custom auth logic for your organization."""
    ...

@catch_mlflow_exception
def _before_request():
    if request.path.startswith("/public"):
        return
    authorization = authenticate_request_custom()
    if isinstance(authorization, Response):
        return authorization

def create_app(app: Flask = app):
    app.add_url_rule("/api/custom-auth/login", view_func=..., methods=["POST"])
    app.before_request(_before_request)
    return app
```

**Entry points** to register in `setup.py`:

```
[mlflow.app]
my-auth=my_auth:create_app
[mlflow.app.client]
my-auth=my_auth:MyAuthClient
```

Then launch with: `mlflow server --app-name my-auth`

## Function-Based Custom Auth

Alternatively, implement a function returning `Authorization` or a `401 Response`, configure it via `auth_config.ini` with `authorization_function = module:function_name`, and start the server with `mlflow server --app-name basic-auth`.

     4→RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl gcc build-essential && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
     5→

Based on the search results, I found comprehensive information about MLflow's RequestAuthProvider plugin:

## MLflow RequestAuthProvider Overview

MLflow provides RequestAuthProvider plugin to customize auth header for outgoing http request.

## Implementation Steps

To use it, implement the RequestAuthProvider class and override the get_name and get_auth methods. get_name should return the name of your auth provider, while get_auth should return the auth object that will be added to the http request.

Here's a basic example:
You can import from mlflow.tracking.request_auth.abstract_request_auth_provider and create a class like DummyAuthProvider that implements get_name() returning a provider name and get_auth() returning the auth object.

## Plugin Registration

Once you have the implemented request auth provider class, register it in the entry_points using "mlflow.request_auth_provider": "dummy-backend=DummyAuthProvider", then set environment variable MLFLOW_TRACKING_AUTH to enable the injection of custom auth.

The entry point configuration shows that the entry point name itself is not used functionally—the entry point name for request auth providers is not used, and so is set to the string "unused" in example configurations like "mlflow.request_auth_provider": "unused=mlflow_test_plugin.request_auth_provider:PluginRequestAuthProvider"

This plugin allows you to implement client-side authentication customization for outgoing HTTP requests from the MLflow client.

## MLflow RequestHeaderProvider Plugin

MLflow exposes a RequestHeaderProvider abstract class to manage OAuth2.0 authentication use cases.

### Python Example Implementation

A custom header provider can be created by inheriting from `RequestHeaderProvider` and implementing methods like `in_context()` and `request_headers()`. Here's the structure from the official MLflow documentation:

```python
from mlflow.tracking.request_header.abstract_request_header_provider import RequestHeaderProvider

class MyHeaderProvider(RequestHeaderProvider):
    """Add custom headers to MLflow requests"""
    def in_context(self):
        return True
    
    def request_headers(self):
        return {
            "X-Client-Version": self._get_client_version(),
            "X-Environment": self._get_environment(),
            "X-User-Agent": "MyOrganization-MLflow-Client",
        }
```

### Using with Cloud Run ID Token

For Cloud Run integration, Google Cloud Run environments have direct support for JWT, and can automatically pass the user's identity in headers when authentication is enabled.

### Entrypoint Plugin Configuration

You can configure a custom request header provider by specifying the path to your class in MLflow configuration, and the class should inherit from the abstract request header provider. The configuration typically involves registering your custom provider as an entrypoint in your plugin's `setup.py` file.

I found search results that cover both `google.oauth2.id_token.fetch_id_token` and metadata server direct requests for Cloud Run. Here's what the documentation shows:

## How `fetch_id_token` Works

When the application is running in Compute Engine, App Engine or Cloud Run, the ID token is obtained from the metadata server. The `google.oauth2.id_token.fetch_id_token()` function is essentially a wrapper that first tries to fetch ID token from the metadata server, and the code works for GAE and Cloud Run metadata server as well.

## Direct Metadata Server Requests

For direct metadata server requests, you can fetch an ID token by making a request to `http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/instance/service-accounts/default/identity?audience=[AUDIENCE]` with the header `Metadata-Flavor: Google`.

## Key Consideration: Token Validity

If you fetch tokens from the metadata server, you will always get a valid token, but if you choose to cache tokens yourself, you can decode the token and check the exp time to see if you need to refresh the token.

## Summary

Both approaches ultimately access the same metadata server when running on Cloud Run. The main difference is that `fetch_id_token()` provides a higher-level abstraction with built-in credential handling, while direct metadata server requests give you more control. The search results don't contain specific performance benchmark comparisons between the two methods, but both are valid approaches for obtaining ID tokens in Cloud Run environments.

content.content:
# Google's Graceful Degradation Recommendations

Based on Google Cloud's official documentation, here are their key recommendations:

## Core Principle
"Graceful degradation is a design approach where a system that experiences a high load continues to function, possibly with reduced performance or accuracy."

## Specific Patterns Recommended

**1. Implement Throttling**
Google recommends using tools like Apigee to control API request rates during high-traffic periods, allowing systems to "scale back requests" rather than failing completely.

**2. Drop Excess Requests Early**
Systems should "drop excess requests at the frontend layer to protect backend components." This prevents cascading failures, though some users may experience errors—a better outcome than total system failure.

**3. Handle Partial Errors and Retries**
Applications should be built to "handle partial errors and retries seamlessly" to maximize traffic served during overload scenarios.

**4. Test Overload Scenarios**
Google stresses regularly simulating overload conditions to validate throttling and request-drop mechanisms work effectively.

**5. Monitor Traffic Spikes**
Using analytics tools to "predict and respond to traffic surges before they escalate into overloads" helps maintain availability during demand peaks.

## Dependency Failure Approach
Rather than the all-or-nothing approach of circuit-breaking, graceful degradation accepts partial functionality, exemplified by Google Search prioritizing higher-ranked results during high load, then resuming full accuracy when conditions normalize.

# Architecture Research: Cloud Run Deployment Reliability

**Domain:** Multi-service GCP Cloud Run deployment with optional observability dependencies
**Researched:** 2026-02-27
**Confidence:** HIGH (codebase analysis) / MEDIUM (Cloud Run patterns from official docs)

## Current System Overview

```
                          Internet
                             |
                +------------+------------+
                |                         |
         +------v------+          +------v------+
         | React SPA   |          | FastAPI API |--------> Vertex AI (Gemini)
         | (Cloud Run) |--------->| (Cloud Run) |--------> GCS (PDF Storage)
         +-------------+  HTTPS   +------+------+
                                         |
                          +--------------+---------------+
                          |              |               |
                   +------v------+ +----v-----+  +------v------+
                   | PostgreSQL  | | OMOP     |  | MLflow      |
                   | (Cloud SQL) | | Vocab DB |  | (Cloud Run) |
                   | REQUIRED    | | REQUIRED |  | OPTIONAL    |
                   +-------------+ +----------+  +------+------+
                                                        |
                                                 +------v------+
                                                 | Cloud SQL   |
                                                 | (mlflow DB) |
                                                 +-------------+
```

### Component Boundaries

| Component | Responsibility | Dependency Class | Current State |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|---------------|
| **FastAPI API** | Gateway for uploads, reviews, exports; hosts outbox processor; runs LangGraph pipeline | Core service | Deployed on Cloud Run, `--allow-unauthenticated` |
| **React Frontend** | Static SPA for human-in-the-loop review | Presentation layer | Deployed on Cloud Run, talks to API via CORS |
| **PostgreSQL (Cloud SQL)** | Primary data store (protocols, criteria, outbox events, audit log) | HARD dependency | Shared instance, `db-f1-micro` |
| **OMOP Vocabulary DB** | Terminology lookup for medical concept grounding | HARD dependency for processing | Same Cloud SQL instance, separate database |
| **LangGraph Processor** | 5-node pipeline: ingest > extract > parse > ground > persist | Runs in-process with API | Triggered by outbox `protocol_uploaded` events |
| **MLflow (Cloud Run)** | Tracing, experiment tracking, observability | SOFT dependency (should be) | Currently treated as HARD in `_preflight_check()` |
| **GCS** | Protocol PDF storage | HARD dependency for uploads/downloads | Has circuit breaker (`gcs_breaker`) |
| **Vertex AI** | MedGemma endpoint for extraction | HARD dependency for processing | Has circuit breaker (`vertex_ai_breaker`) |

## The Core Problem: Dependency Classification

The fundamental architectural issue is that MLflow is classified as a **hard dependency** in the code despite being an **observability tool**. This creates a cascade:

```
MLflow 503/403 at startup or runtime
    |
    +---> _preflight_check() raises DependencyCheckError
    |         |
    |         +---> Pipeline never starts
    |         +---> Outbox event retries 3x then dead_letters
    |         +---> Protocol stuck in "extraction_failed"
    |
    +---> MLflow trace export hangs/retries
    |         |
    |         +---> Threads consumed by HTTP requests to dead MLflow
    |         +---> API responsiveness degrades
    |
    +---> Cold start: MLflow Cloud Run instance may take 30s+
              |
              +---> API startup init thread waits (already mitigated with daemon thread)
              +---> First pipeline run hits preflight timeout
```

**Where the code enforces this hard dependency (3 locations):**

1. `trigger.py:_preflight_check()` lines 329-359 -- checks MLflow health, raises `DependencyCheckError` if down
2. `trigger.py:_cleanup_orphan_traces()` lines 35-85 -- runs at module import, calls MLflow client
3. `trigger.py:_ensure_mlflow()` lines 107-149 -- called before every pipeline run

## Recommended Architecture: Dependency Tiers

Classify every external dependency into one of three tiers:

### Tier 1: REQUIRED (blocks startup + request serving)

Services without which the API cannot serve any requests.

| Service | Why Required | Health Check Impact |
|---------|-------------|---------------------|
| PostgreSQL (main DB) | All data reads/writes, session state, outbox | `/health` returns 503 |
| OMOP Vocabulary DB | Required for grounding step in pipeline | `/ready` returns 503 |

### Tier 2: REQUIRED-FOR-PROCESSING (blocks pipeline, not API)

Services without which the pipeline cannot run, but the API can still serve reads/reviews/exports.

| Service | Why Required for Processing | Degraded Behavior |
|---------|---------------------------|-------------------|
| Vertex AI (Gemini) | LLM extraction + structuring | Pipeline skips, protocol shows "service unavailable" |
| GCS | PDF retrieval for ingest step | Upload still queued, processing deferred |

### Tier 3: OPTIONAL (never blocks anything)

Services whose absence degrades observability but not functionality.

| Service | What Degrades | Graceful Behavior |
|---------|---------------|-------------------|
| MLflow | No trace export, no experiment tracking | Silent no-op; log warning once |

## Architectural Patterns to Implement

### Pattern 1: Circuit Breaker with No-Op Fallback for MLflow

**What:** Wrap all MLflow interactions behind a circuit breaker that falls back to no-ops when MLflow is unreachable. The existing `pybreaker` infrastructure already supports this pattern.

**Why:** The codebase already has circuit breakers for Gemini, GCS, Vertex AI, and ToolUniverse (in `shared/resilience.py`), but MLflow has none. MLflow is the only service that can block the entire pipeline despite being observability-only.

**Implementation:**

```python
# shared/resilience.py -- add MLflow breaker
mlflow_breaker = CircuitBreaker(
    fail_max=3,
    reset_timeout=120,  # Longer recovery: MLflow cold starts take 30s+
    name="mlflow",
    listeners=[_mlflow_listener],
)
```

```python
# protocol_processor/tracing.py -- wrap span creation
from shared.resilience import mlflow_breaker
from pybreaker import CircuitBreakerError

@contextmanager
def pipeline_span(name, span_type="CHAIN", protocol_id=""):
    try:
        if not os.getenv("MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI"):
            yield _NoOpSpan()
            return
        # Circuit breaker prevents hammering a dead MLflow
        @mlflow_breaker
        def _create_span():
            import mlflow
            return mlflow.start_span(name=name, span_type=span_type)

        with _create_span() as span:
            yield span
            return
    except (CircuitBreakerError, Exception):
        yield _NoOpSpan()
```

**Confidence:** HIGH -- pybreaker is already a project dependency, pattern matches existing breakers.

### Pattern 2: Remove MLflow from Preflight Check

**What:** Remove the MLflow health check from `_preflight_check()` in `trigger.py`. The preflight should only check Tier 1 and Tier 2 dependencies.

**Why:** The preflight's purpose is to avoid wasting Gemini/ToolUniverse API calls on a pipeline that will fail anyway. MLflow being down does not cause pipeline failure -- it only means traces are not recorded.

**Current code (lines 329-359 of trigger.py):**
```python
# 3. MLflow tracking server (required for observability)  <-- WRONG classification
tracking_uri = os.getenv("MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI")
if not tracking_uri:
    raise DependencyCheckError(
        "MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI environment variable is not set"
    )
```

**Target state:**
```python
# 3. MLflow tracking server (OPTIONAL -- best-effort, never blocks pipeline)
tracking_uri = os.getenv("MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI")
if tracking_uri:
    try:
        # Non-blocking check; log warning if down but continue
        req = urllib.request.Request(f"{tracking_uri}/health", method="GET")
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=2) as resp:
            if resp.status >= 400:
                logger.warning("MLflow health check returned %d (non-fatal)", resp.status)
    except Exception:
        logger.warning("MLflow unreachable (non-fatal), traces disabled for this run")
```

**Confidence:** HIGH -- directly addresses the stated problem.

### Pattern 3: Cloud Run Startup/Liveness Probes for Tiered Health

**What:** Configure Cloud Run health probes that only check Tier 1 dependencies, keeping the API routable even when Tier 3 services are down.

**Cloud Run probe configuration:**

| Probe | Endpoint | Checks | Purpose |
|-------|----------|--------|---------|
| Startup | `GET /health` | PostgreSQL only | Container ready to receive requests |
| Liveness | `GET /health` | PostgreSQL only | Container still responsive |
| Readiness (app-level) | `GET /ready` | PostgreSQL + OMOP | Full processing capability |

**Current state:** The `/health` endpoint already correctly returns 503 only when the main DB is down and treats OMOP/GCS/breakers as informational. This is well-designed for Cloud Run startup/liveness probes.

**What to add to `gcloud run deploy`:**
```bash
gcloud run deploy api \
  ... \
  --startup-cpu-boost \
  --cpu-throttling \
  --startup-probe-type=http \
  --startup-probe-path=/health \
  --startup-probe-initial-delay=5 \
  --startup-probe-period=10 \
  --startup-probe-failure-threshold=6 \
  --startup-probe-timeout=5 \
  --liveness-probe-type=http \
  --liveness-probe-path=/health \
  --liveness-probe-period=30 \
  --liveness-probe-failure-threshold=3 \
  --liveness-probe-timeout=5
```

**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- probe flags verified from official Cloud Run docs. Exact flag names should be confirmed against `gcloud run deploy --help` at deploy time, as the CLI evolves.

### Pattern 4: Service-to-Service Auth Token Refresh

**What:** The existing `_cloud_run_auth.py` caches ID tokens with a 5-minute refresh margin. This is correct but fragile -- the token is stored in `os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN"]` and never refreshed during long pipeline runs.

**Current issue:** A pipeline run can take 5-30 minutes. If the cached token expires mid-run, MLflow trace exports will fail with 403. Since there is no circuit breaker on MLflow, these 403s cause retries that consume threads.

**Recommended improvement:**
```python
# _cloud_run_auth.py -- add a refresh-on-use wrapper
import functools

def with_fresh_token(func):
    """Decorator that refreshes the MLflow ID token before each call."""
    @functools.wraps(func)
    def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
        tracking_uri = os.getenv("MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI")
        if tracking_uri and _is_cloud_run():
            token = get_id_token(tracking_uri)  # Returns cached if still valid
            if token:
                os.environ["MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN"] = token
        return func(*args, **kwargs)
    return wrapper
```

**But more importantly:** With MLflow behind a circuit breaker, token refresh failures become non-fatal. The circuit opens after 3 failures, and traces silently degrade to no-ops.

**Confidence:** HIGH -- matches Cloud Run metadata server patterns from official docs.

### Pattern 5: Async MLflow Export with Bounded Queue

**What:** MLflow 3.x supports async trace logging by default in production. The codebase should ensure this is enabled and add a bounded queue to prevent memory growth when MLflow is slow/down.

**Why:** When MLflow returns 503, synchronous trace export blocks the calling thread. With the outbox processor's 2-worker thread pool, just 2 stuck MLflow calls can deadlock all pipeline processing.

**Configuration:**
```python
# Set via environment variables in deploy script
MLFLOW_ENABLE_ASYNC_LOGGING=true        # Already default in MLflow 3.x
MLFLOW_ASYNC_LOGGING_QUEUE_SIZE=100     # Bound the queue; drop traces if full
MLFLOW_ASYNC_LOGGING_WORKER_COUNT=2     # Limit threads used for export
```

**Confidence:** MEDIUM -- MLflow 3.x async logging behavior confirmed via MLflow docs, but exact env var names should be verified against the deployed MLflow version (v2.19.0 in Dockerfile vs v3.9.0 in docker-compose).

**Note:** The Dockerfile uses MLflow v2.19.0 (`ghcr.io/mlflow/mlflow:v2.19.0`) while docker-compose uses v3.9.0. This version mismatch itself is a deployment issue. The Cloud Run deployment should be upgraded to v3.x for async logging support.

## Data Flow

### Protocol Upload Flow (Happy Path)

```
User uploads PDF
    |
    v
[POST /protocols] ---> Save to GCS + Write Protocol row + Outbox event
    |                   (single DB transaction via persist_with_outbox)
    v
[OutboxProcessor] ---> poll_and_process() picks up "protocol_uploaded"
    |                   (runs in ThreadPoolExecutor, max_workers=2)
    v
[handle_protocol_uploaded]
    |
    +---> _preflight_check()  <-- Currently checks DB, OMOP, MLflow
    +---> _ensure_mlflow()    <-- Sets experiment for this thread
    |
    v
[asyncio.run(_run_pipeline)]
    |
    +---> ingest_node    ---> Read PDF from GCS
    +---> extract_node   ---> Gemini LLM call (via Vertex AI)
    +---> parse_node     ---> Structure extraction output
    +---> ground_node    ---> OMOP vocabulary lookup + UMLS grounding
    +---> persist_node   ---> Write criteria + entities to PostgreSQL
    |
    v
Protocol status: "extracted" (or "extraction_failed")
```

### Degraded Flow (MLflow Down)

**Target state after fixes:**

```
[handle_protocol_uploaded]
    |
    +---> _preflight_check()  ---> Checks DB + OMOP only
    +---> _ensure_mlflow()    ---> Returns False (MLflow unreachable)
    |                              Logs warning, continues
    v
[asyncio.run(_run_pipeline)]
    |
    +---> pipeline_span()     ---> mlflow_breaker OPEN
    |                              Yields _NoOpSpan immediately
    +---> llm_span()          ---> Same: no-op fallback
    |
    v
Pipeline completes normally, no traces recorded
```

### Service Communication Map

```
                  Service-to-Service Auth
                  (ID token from metadata server)
                           |
React SPA ---HTTPS---> FastAPI API ---HTTPS---> MLflow (Cloud Run)
                           |                        |
                           |                  (MLFLOW_TRACKING_TOKEN
                           |                   in Authorization header)
                           |
                    +------+------+------+
                    |      |      |      |
                   SQL    SQL   gRPC   HTTPS
                    |      |      |      |
                   Main   OMOP  Vertex  GCS
                    DB    Vocab   AI
```

## Anti-Patterns to Avoid

### Anti-Pattern 1: Observability Dependency Blocking Core Function

**What people do:** Treat monitoring/tracing services as required for application function. Check their health in preflight, fail the pipeline if they are down.

**Why it is wrong:** Observability tools exist to observe the system, not to be part of it. When observability blocks functionality, you get the worst of both worlds: the system is down AND you cannot trace why.

**Do this instead:** All MLflow interactions must be fire-and-forget with circuit breaker protection. Log a warning when MLflow is unreachable. Never raise exceptions from tracing code. Never block startup or processing on tracing availability.

### Anti-Pattern 2: Module-Level Side Effects Calling External Services

**What people do:** Call external services at module import time (e.g., `_cleanup_orphan_traces()` at line 89 of `trigger.py` runs at import).

**Why it is wrong:** Module imports happen during application startup. If the external service is down, the import either blocks or raises, potentially preventing the entire application from starting. This is especially dangerous on Cloud Run where cold starts are common.

**Do this instead:** Defer all external service calls to explicit initialization functions called from the lifespan handler. Make them async or run them in background threads. The current `_deferred_mlflow_init` in `main.py` already does this correctly for MLflow init -- but `_cleanup_orphan_traces()` at module scope in `trigger.py` circumvents it.

### Anti-Pattern 3: Unbounded Retry Against a Down Service

**What people do:** Let HTTP clients retry indefinitely (or with long timeouts) against a service returning 503.

**Why it is wrong:** Each retry consumes a thread. With a 2-worker thread pool (outbox processor), just 2 stuck retries deadlock all pipeline processing. On Cloud Run, this manifests as the API instance using all its CPU on blocked threads while appearing "healthy" to the load balancer.

**Do this instead:** Circuit breaker with fail_max=3 and reset_timeout=120s. Fail fast when the circuit is open. Use short HTTP timeouts (2-5 seconds) for non-critical services.

## Integration Points

### External Services

| Service | Integration Pattern | Critical Notes |
|---------|---------------------|----------------|
| Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) | Unix socket via Cloud SQL Proxy sidecar (`/cloudsql/CONNECTION_NAME`) | Cloud Run auto-injects proxy. Secrets via Secret Manager. |
| GCS | google-cloud-storage SDK with circuit breaker | `gcs_breaker` already exists. Token from default credentials. |
| Vertex AI | google-cloud-aiplatform SDK with circuit breaker | `vertex_ai_breaker` exists. Needs `roles/aiplatform.user`. |
| MLflow (Cloud Run) | HTTP REST via `mlflow` Python SDK | Needs ID token for service-to-service auth. Currently `--allow-unauthenticated` (see Security note). |
| Gemini API | google-generativeai SDK with circuit breaker | `gemini_breaker` exists. API key via Secret Manager. |

### Security Concern: MLflow `--allow-unauthenticated`

The MLflow Cloud Run service is deployed with `--allow-unauthenticated`. This means anyone with the service URL can read all experiment traces and data. This should be changed to require IAM authentication (`--no-allow-unauthenticated`), with the API service account granted `roles/run.invoker` on the MLflow service. The `_cloud_run_auth.py` module already handles ID token acquisition for this pattern.

### Internal Boundaries

| Boundary | Communication | Notes |
|----------|---------------|-------|
| API <-> Protocol Processor | In-process via outbox event handlers | Same Python process; `handle_protocol_uploaded` called synchronously by outbox |
| API <-> Frontend | HTTPS REST | CORS configured via `CORS_ORIGINS` env var |
| Protocol Processor <-> MLflow | HTTP (mlflow SDK) | Should be behind circuit breaker; currently unbounded |
| All services <-> Secret Manager | gcloud metadata + IAM | Secrets injected at deploy time via `--set-secrets` |

## Scaling Considerations

| Scale | Architecture Adjustments |
|-------|--------------------------|
| Current (1-10 users) | Single API instance, 2 outbox workers, in-process pipeline. Fine as-is. |
| 10-50 users | Increase `max_instances` on API Cloud Run. Pipeline throughput limited by 2-worker thread pool -- increase to 4. |
| 50+ concurrent protocols | Move pipeline to separate Cloud Run service (or Cloud Run Jobs). Outbox publishes to Pub/Sub; pipeline service subscribes. This decouples API responsiveness from pipeline processing. |

### Scaling Priorities

1. **First bottleneck: Outbox processor thread pool (max_workers=2).** Two simultaneous protocol uploads saturate all workers. Long-running pipelines (5-30 min) hold threads for the entire duration. Fix: increase workers or move to async pipeline execution.

2. **Second bottleneck: Cloud SQL connection limits.** `db-f1-micro` supports ~25 connections. API + outbox + MLflow backend all share the same instance. Fix: connection pooling at app level (SQLAlchemy pool_size) and consider upgrading to `db-g1-small`.

## Build Order for Reliability Milestone

Based on the dependency analysis, the recommended build order is:

### Phase 1: Decouple MLflow (Highest Impact, Lowest Risk)

1. Add `mlflow_breaker` to `shared/resilience.py`
2. Remove MLflow from `_preflight_check()` in `trigger.py`
3. Move `_cleanup_orphan_traces()` from module-scope to deferred init
4. Wrap `pipeline_span()` and `llm_span()` with circuit breaker fallback

**Rationale:** This is the single change that resolves all three stated problems (403 blocks startup, 503 consumes threads, preflight requires MLflow). Minimal code changes, high confidence, no infrastructure changes needed.

### Phase 2: Harden Service-to-Service Auth

1. Switch MLflow Cloud Run from `--allow-unauthenticated` to `--no-allow-unauthenticated`
2. Grant API service account `roles/run.invoker` on MLflow service
3. Add token refresh to MLflow circuit breaker (refresh before retry in half-open state)

**Rationale:** Fixes the security concern and ensures auth failures trigger the circuit breaker rather than causing silent data loss.

### Phase 3: Health Probe Configuration

1. Add explicit Cloud Run startup and liveness probes (HTTP on `/health`)
2. Verify `/health` only fails on Tier 1 dependencies (already correct)
3. Add MLflow status to `/health` as informational (breaker state)

**Rationale:** Prevents Cloud Run from routing traffic to instances that are genuinely unhealthy, while not falsely marking instances as unhealthy due to MLflow.

### Phase 4: Version Alignment and Async Logging

1. Upgrade MLflow Cloud Run image from v2.19.0 to v3.x
2. Align with docker-compose (v3.9.0) for local-cloud parity
3. Enable async trace logging in production
4. Set bounded queue size to prevent memory growth

**Rationale:** Depends on Phase 1 (circuit breaker) being in place first. Async logging reduces thread contention but does not eliminate the need for circuit breaking.

## Sources

- [Google Cloud: Design for graceful degradation](https://docs.google.com/architecture/framework/reliability/graceful-degradation) -- MEDIUM confidence, general guidance not Cloud Run-specific
- [Google Cloud: Configure container health checks for services](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/healthchecks) -- HIGH confidence, official Cloud Run docs
- [Google Cloud: Authenticating service-to-service](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/authenticating/service-to-service) -- HIGH confidence, official Cloud Run docs
- [Google Cloud: Best practices for using service accounts securely](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-service-accounts) -- HIGH confidence, official IAM docs
- [MLflow: Production Tracing and Monitoring](https://mlflow.org/docs/latest/genai/tracing/prod-tracing/) -- MEDIUM confidence, MLflow official docs
- [pybreaker PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/pybreaker/) -- HIGH confidence, already used in project
- Codebase analysis of `trigger.py`, `main.py`, `middleware.py`, `resilience.py`, `_cloud_run_auth.py`, `outbox.py`, `tracing.py` -- HIGH confidence, direct code reading
